mentl/bd4fac9:
Two on-disk data validators, cross-validated against numpy/python, each
stressing a different representation the m3==m4 fixpoint is structurally
blind to (a byte-identical wheel can still corrupt user data, so only an
independent implementation over the same bytes catches it).

stats-float reads 400 sensor-like samples and computes three DISCRETE
facts: the argmin index, the argmax index, and the count of samples above
the mean. Discrete facts carry no transcendental, so Mentl and numpy must
agree exactly (argmin 137, argmax 298, above-mean 199). It exercises a
different set of [Float] paths than CFC: a fold-sum mean and
comparison-reduction, not trig and DFT.

text-bytes reads a 429-byte prose corpus and computes the byte count, the
count of 'e' and 't', and the most frequent lowercase letter by a 256-slot
Int histogram argmax. This is the first end-to-end validator for the
String=[byte] merge on real text: byte_len, byte_at, structural == over
every byte, and list_set/list_index into a histogram (count_e 47,
count_t 32, top 'e').

Both use annotated accumulators and inline lambdas — the forms that
specialize per call site at the concrete representation. Seen RED first:
reversed stats data shifts numpy and Mentl together to argmin 262 (exit 1),
and extra text shifts the byte count off 429 (exit 1), so the assertions
are data-driven, never constants the gate always sees.

Adds the io-rec link mode (base runtime + WASI fs, run preopens /tmp) and
run_data_validator, a generic wrapper that copies a committed fixture to
/tmp, asserts Mentl's exit 42, then asserts the oracle's EXPECTED_<key>
facts over the same bytes (skipped-noted when the oracle's deps are
absent). Frontier 144 pass / 0 red.

perennials/bd02f50:
The capture flow Morgan asked for: tap the sheet where you know a rise
or a dip, type its metres (signed, units allowed, 0 is the level you
stand on), and a surveyor's benchmark lands in her sepia. Tap a
benchmark to change or remove its height, drag it to move it with its
number riding along. Every edit is a whole-yard commit, so undo
un-draws the land exactly like ink. A few taps and the yard has a
shape; refining later is the same gesture again.

The tabs learn two things. The projection toggle now appears once
anything stands — a plant, or ground she has shaped — because shaping
the land before planting it is the honest order of the work. And the
sheet's whole workbench (tool seg, the active tool's input row, the
photo row) moves from below the year scrubber to directly under the
paper, where the thumb already is; the reading controls follow after.

The ground's coverage line prints under the side and model views: how
many heights shape it, and that it settles level where she set none.
Nothing renders differently on a yard that never used the tool.

noodles/bdcbcc5:
init() sat on an unexplained wait(400) after the primer already did its
job and after the drum samples had preloaded (loadSamples runs at graph
build, so first play awaits a settled promise, not a fetch). It bought
nothing — just a dead gap before the first sound and the pie timers.

Measured press -> first pie movement: 1041ms -> 625ms. The primer stays
(it's the part that keeps the first notes from being swallowed by the
hardware ramp-up); the lookahead and start-lead stay (weak-core
stability). First-play only — later plays skip init entirely.

While chasing this, confirmed the pie timers are NOT the problem: the
clock emits progress every 16th, the sweep is tempo-locked, and the loop
pie wraps every 2050ms against 2000ms expected (consistent, not
drifting) — real-time synced. The felt "messing with the pies" was this
startup gap, not a cadence bug.
noodles/bd3e047:
Three ways they were off. They never filled — progress was elapsed-at-
step-start, topping out at 15/16ths before snapping to zero, so the
dial always read as resetting early; it now targets completion of the
sounding step and hits 100% exactly on the wrap. They led the ear —
beat visuals fired on the transport clock while the sound arrived an
output-latency later (large under latencyHint:playback, larger on
Bluetooth); beat-synced draws now shift by the context's reported
output latency. And they jumped in 16th steps — --pct is a registered
custom property that transitions over one 16th (--stepdur tracks the
tempo), with a snap class so the wrap jumps back instead of sweeping
backwards. Unsupported browsers just keep the per-step jump.
